No worries — big O can feel silly at first. Here’s a down-to-earth way to think about it, kid-friendly style, then some quick examples you can actually use for your studying.

Big picture idea
- Big O is about how the time (or space) grows as the input gets bigger.
- We care about the worst case, and we ignore tiny constant factors and tiny slowdowns.
- So we say something is O(n) if doubling the input roughly doubles the work; O(log n) if it grows really slowly; O(n log n) is in-between; etc.

Tiny glossary to get comfy
- O(1): constant work, no matter how big n is. Like “look up the first item in an array by index” — same time every time.
- O(log n): grows slowly. Like “asking yes/no questions that cut the remaining options in half each time.” Each question halves the problem, so you only need about log2(n) questions.
- O(n): linear. Do something once for every item: n items → n steps.
- O(n log n): a mix. Do something for each item, but that something itself costs about log n steps. So n × log n total.
- O(n^2): quadratic. Nested loops over n items: for each item you do roughly n more steps. Often seen when you have two loops from 1 to n.
- O(2^n) or O(n!): grow very fast. Not great for big n.

Simple, concrete examples
- O(log n): Binary search
  - You have a sorted list of n items. You ask: “Is the target in the left half or the right half?” Each question halves the remaining list. After about log2(n) questions, you find it or decide it isn’t there. So O(log n).

- O(n): Scanning a list
  - Look at each item once to see if it matches something. If there are n items, you do about n checks.

- O(n log n): Sorting with a typical divide-and-conquer sort (like mergesort or heapsort)
  - The big idea: the problem is broken into halves repeatedly (log n levels), and at each level you do linear work (n) to merge or organize. So you get n × log n total.

- O(n^2): Nested loops
  - If you have two loops, both going from 1 to n, you do roughly n × n steps. E.g., checking all pairs of items.

Amortized analysis in plain language
- What it is: look at a sequence of many operations, and ask “average cost per operation” over that whole sequence.
- Why it helps: some operations can be expensive, but if they’re rare, the average cost stays small.

Classic example: dynamic arrays (like a grown-up growable list)
- Suppose you start with capacity 1. When you add an item and there’s no room, you resize to capacity 2, then 4, then 8, etc.
- The expensive steps (resizing) happen, but they don’t happen every time you add something.
- If you add N items, the total cost is about a constant multiple of N (the occasional big resize is “paid for” by many cheap adds). So the amortized cost per add is O(1), even though a single add could be O(n) during a resize.
- Intuition: over a long run, the expensive steps are spread out so thin that they don’t push the average above a constant.

How to analyze a problem quickly (practical quick guide)
- Look for loops:
  - One loop over n -> O(n).
  - Nested loops over n -> O(n^2) (sometimes it’s less if inner loops don’t run all the time; need details).
- Look for multiple big factors:
  - For each of n items, you do something that costs m steps -> O(n × m). If m is about log n, you get O(n log n).
- For recursion (divide and conquer):
  - If you split the problem in half and do O(n) work outside the recursion, you often get O(n log n).
  - If you split and do a little constant work outside, you sometimes get O(n).
  - The Master Theorem is a standard tool you’ll see in class; your midterm might touch the basic cases.

- O(log n) grows slow (halving).
- O(n) grows linear (one thing per item).
- O(n log n) is “linear times log”: think n items, each with a tiny log n cost.
- O(1) is constant, O(n^2) is nested linear, etc.
- Amortized analysis looks at the average cost per operation over many operations, not just the worst single operation.

Big idea recap
- Merge sort splits the array in half, halves again, until you’re down to single elements.
- Then it merges those pieces back together, always creating a bigger sorted piece from two sorted halves.
- The key: there are multiple "levels" of merging, and each level touches every element a constant number of times. The number of levels is what gives you the log n.

- How many times can you halve n until you reach 1? About log2 n times. That count is the depth of the recursion (the number of levels of splitting).
- At each level, you’re merging many small sorted pieces to form bigger sorted pieces.

- Since there are log n levels and each level costs about c·n operations, total cost is c·n·log2 n. Hence O(n log n).
